• By vote, I mean in the election that selects the party/person who will run your country for the next term (i.e federal/national/presidential/whatever election).
  • You would be selling your vote for only one election (not ongoing).
  • You would be selling all of your votes/options for that election (i.e. some countries elect both upper and lower houses, have preferential voting, etc.; selling your vote would be allowing someone else to choose all of this for one election).
  • If you feel comfortable, also state what country you're from (will be interesting to see if different countries value their votes more/less).
If it was legal to sell your vote, would you sell it, and how much would you be willing to settle for?

Hmm. Idk, this is really simplified and I'm sure there are lots of interesting situations one could look at. What do others think?

You raise some interesting points there.

In the vast majority of cases, a single vote won't decide an election. If the number of people willing to sell votes was very small, those votes presumably wouldn't be worth much, as they would be relatively ineffective (this is one of the few scenarios I can think of that runs contrary to supply and demand). If the votes for sale in the electorate was larger than the margin between the front-running candidates, though, these votes would probably be worth a lot of money as they could decide the outcome. As you pointed out, though, the more skewed an electorate is, the more likely that the people selling their votes will be the supporters of parties very unlikely to win, so there would be little point in those parties buying the votes, and the value of the votes would be very low due to the lack of competition/demand. Another thing to factor is that if an election for an electorate was tight/close (i.e. two front-runners with ~50% of the vote), for every 2 votes each party buys, it is likely that 1 would have been from someone who would have voted for them anyway (i.e. votes have half their perceived value). That of course ignores the fact that certain areas or demographics of an electorate may be more likely to vote for a given party, consequently opposition parties may target those areas/demographics in their vote buying. By the same logic, parties may use this information to decide how much they were willing to pay someone for their vote (an unemployed person would probably be more willing to sell their vote for $1000 than a person earning a large salary, etc.).

It's very interesting to think of this on a macro scale, as you did. Wealth would determine elections, but in that determination there would be a redistribution of that wealth. The calculation by the wealthy would be an ROI: by electing a given party, will the financial benefit to them be greater than the outlay of the vote buying. It would be very interesting to see how that played out.
